title: Apprenticeship vs Internship: What's the Difference, and Which Should You Choose?
summary: Apprenticeship vs internship: compare pay, length, sponsors and credentials, plus registered and degree apprenticeships and where each goes on a resume.
body_markdown:
The apprenticeship vs internship question sounds like vocabulary. It's really about commitment. An apprenticeship is a paid job with training built in, and it usually lasts years. An internship is a short look at a field. One summer, usually.


We sit down with a lot of students one-on-one, and we hear the two words swapped all the time. They aren't the same thing. Mixing them up costs people. Some students scroll past apprenticeship postings because they assume those are only for electricians. Others expect an internship to come with the pay and the credential that only an apprenticeship promises.


So this guide compares the two using the U.S. Department of Labor's own rules and numbers, then shows where each one belongs on your resume.


## TL;DR


• An apprenticeship is a paid job with structured training that usually runs one to three years and ends in a recognized credential. An internship is a short work experience, usually one to three months, that may or may not be paid.


• Registered apprentices get scheduled raises as their skills grow, and 94% of those who finish stay employed at an average salary of $84,000, according to the U.S. Department of Labor. Interns at the bachelor's level average $23.35 an hour, according to NACE.


• Registered apprenticeships are approved by the Department of Labor or a state agency, while internships are run by individual employers and nobody registers them.


• Degree apprenticeships are growing: New America found 579 of them at 346 US colleges in 2025.


• Both are verified by the employer, so both go under Experience on a resume.


[Externships](https://www.extern.com/post/what-is-an-externship) are short, remote professional experience programs where you work on real projects with real companies. If you'd like to try a field before committing to either path, the[Hydroficient IoT Cyber Defense Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/hydroficient-iot-cyber-defense-externship-nov-2026) , the[TruBridge Healthcare Data Analytics Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/trubridge-healthcare-data-analytics-externship-nov-2026) and the[Wayfair n8n AI Agent Engineering Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/wayfair-ai-agent-engineering-for-business-intelligence-nov-2026) are open now.[Explore all Externships](https://www.extern.com/externships) .

## What Is the Difference Between an Apprenticeship and an Internship?


An apprenticeship trains you for one occupation while paying you to do it. An internship lets you sample a field for a few weeks. The[U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/help/what-difference-between-apprenticeship-and-internship) puts the typical lengths at one to three years for apprenticeships and one to three months for internships.


### What Is an Apprenticeship?


An **apprenticeship** is a paid job that combines structured on-the-job training with related classroom instruction and ends in a recognized credential. In the US, a **Registered Apprenticeship** is a program that's been approved by the Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency, so the training plan, the wage schedule and the credential all meet a national standard.


The Department of Labor's[career seeker fact sheet](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/sites/default/files/DOL_IndustryFS_CareerSeeker_031125.pdf) lists five components that every registered program has:


1. **Industry led.** Employers and industry groups vet the program, so the training matches what the work requires.


2. **Paid job.** You're an employee, and your wage rises as your skills and productivity grow.


3. **Structured on-the-job learning.** You train at work under an experienced mentor.


4. **Supplemental education.** Classroom instruction covers the theory behind the work, and it often earns college credit.


5. **Credentials.** You finish with a portable, nationally recognized credential in your industry.


### What Is an Internship?


An **internship** is a short, supervised work experience, usually one to three months, that lets a student or recent graduate try out a field. It can be paid or unpaid, full-time or part-time, in person or remote. There's no federal definition. The Department of Labor says it doesn't have an official one for internships.


Internships come in many versions, and we sort through them in our guide to the[types of internships compared](https://www.extern.com/post/what-is-an-internship-types) .


The core contrast is purpose. An internship is built for exposure: you're there to see how a team works and whether you'd want the job. An apprenticeship assumes you've already decided.


### Apprenticeship vs Internship at a Glance


Put side by side, the two formats differ on almost every practical point: how long they last, whether pay is guaranteed, who's responsible for your training and what you walk away with.


Feature Registered apprenticeship Internship


**Typical length** 1 to 3 years 1 to 3 months


**Pay** Always paid, with scheduled raises Paid or unpaid. Bachelor's-level interns average $23.35 an hour (NACE, 2026)


**Employment status** Employee from day one Temporary role. An unpaid intern may not legally be an employee


**Training** Structured on-the-job learning plus classroom instruction Varies by employer, often informal


**Who runs it** An employer or program sponsor, approved by the Department of Labor or a state agency The employer. No registration


**What you leave with** A nationally recognized credential and, usually, a job Experience, references and sometimes a full-time offer


**Best for** People committed to one occupation Students still comparing fields


**Shows up in a background check** Yes, the employer verifies it Yes, the employer verifies it


**Resume section** Experience, with the credential under Certifications Experience

## Do Apprenticeships and Internships Pay?


Registered apprenticeships always pay, because they're jobs. Internships often pay, but not always, and the difference comes down to employment law.


### How Apprentice Pay Works


Registered apprentices are paid from the first day, and the raises are written into the program. Federal apprenticeship standards ([29 CFR 29.5](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/29.5) ) require a wage schedule that goes up as the apprentice gains skills, and the starting wage can't be lower than the federal minimum wage where that law applies.


According to the Department of Labor fact sheet linked above (updated March 2025), 94% of apprentices who complete a registered program stay employed, with an average annual salary of $84,000.


But read that number carefully. It describes people who finished. Starting wages are lower, and they vary a lot by occupation and region.


One qualification, since we said "always." That's true of registered programs. A company can call any training role an apprenticeship, so check that yours is registered.


### How Intern Pay Works


Intern pay depends on the employer. According to NACE's[2026 Guide to Compensation for Interns & Co-ops](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/internships/hourly-wage-for-interns-climbs-but-is-down-over-last-10-years-in-real-terms) , interns at the bachelor's level earned an average of $23.35 an hour, based on what employers reported paying as of summer 2025.


But not every internship pays. A for-profit employer can offer an unpaid internship only when the intern, not the company, is the main beneficiary of the arrangement. The Department of Labor's[Fact Sheet #71](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/71-flsa-internships) sets out a "primary beneficiary test" with seven factors. If the test shows you're working as an employee, you're owed minimum wage and overtime.


Our guide on[whether interns get paid](https://www.extern.com/post/do-you-get-paid-in-an-internship-guide) goes deeper into pay by industry.


---


## How Long Does Each One Last, and Who Runs It?


Length is the biggest practical difference between the two, and it follows from who's in charge. A registered apprenticeship answers to a national standard. An internship answers to one employer.


### Length and Time Commitment


An apprenticeship is measured in years. An internship is measured in weeks.


The sources line up on this:


• That same Department of Labor comparison describes internships as short term and apprenticeships as longer term.


• Under 29 CFR 29.5, a registered apprenticeship measured by time requires at least 2,000 hours of on-the-job learning. That's roughly a year of full-time work, and plenty of programs run longer.


• The same regulation recommends at least 144 hours of related classroom instruction for each year of the program.


Some programs measure competency instead, so you finish when you've shown the skills.


And that's the trade-off. A summer internship that turns out to be a poor fit costs you ten weeks. Leaving an apprenticeship halfway means leaving a job and an unfinished credential behind.


### Who Sponsors Registered Apprenticeships, and How to Find One


A registered apprenticeship has two layers. An employer or program sponsor hires and trains you. A government body, either the Department of Labor or a State Apprenticeship Agency, approves the program.


Think it's only for the trades? The Department of Labor lists registered programs in technology, healthcare, financial services, advanced manufacturing, construction, energy, education and several other industries.


Here's how to find one and apply:


1. **Search the Apprenticeship Finder.** The[Apprenticeship Finder on Apprenticeship.gov](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/apprenticeship-job-finder) lets you enter an occupation and a location to see open apprenticeship postings from employers nationwide.


2. **Check the entry requirements.** Federal standards set the minimum starting age at 16, and each sponsor adds its own qualifications.


3. **Apply directly with the employer or sponsor.** There's no central application, so each posting tells you who to contact.


4. **Ask two questions before you accept.** What's the wage schedule, and which credential will you hold when you finish?


Internships work differently. No agency registers them. The employer designs the program, posts it on its careers page or a job board and decides what you'll do. Our list of the[best websites to find internships](https://www.extern.com/post/best-websites-to-find-internships) covers where those postings show up.

## What Is a Degree Apprenticeship?


A **degree apprenticeship** is a registered apprenticeship joined to a college degree. You work in a paid role, take coursework tied to that role, and finish with both a degree and an apprenticeship credential.


### Degree Apprenticeships in the US


The model is new here, but it isn't rare anymore. According to New America's January 2026 report,[Mapping the Landscape of Degree Apprenticeship](https://www.newamerica.org/education-policy/reports/mapping-the-landscape-of-degree-apprenticeship-expanding-a-promising-model-for-mobility/) , 346 colleges and universities in 49 states and Washington, D.C. offered 579 degree apprenticeship opportunities as of summer 2025.


Look past the headline, though. About two-thirds of those opportunities lead to an associate degree, 29% lead to a bachelor's degree and 4% lead to a master's degree. The two most common occupations are K-12 teacher and registered nurse.


So if you're picturing a degree apprenticeship in software development, they do appear in New America's data, but most of what exists today is in education and health care. We're not sure how quickly that will change.


### How the UK Model Compares


Search for "degree apprenticeship" and many of the results are British. In England,[GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/become-apprentice) describes degree apprenticeships as Levels 6 and 7, equivalent to a bachelor's or master's degree, with at least 20% of normal working hours set aside for training.


The US has no national ladder like that, so your options depend on your state and field.


---


## Which One Is Right for You?


Choose the apprenticeship if you know the occupation you want. Choose the internship if you're still testing options or you're enrolled full-time.


That's the short version.


### When an Apprenticeship Fits and When an Internship Fits


**An apprenticeship fits when:**


• **You've chosen an occupation.** The whole program is built around one role, so it rewards certainty.


• **You need a paycheck now.** You earn from day one, and you don't take on debt for the training.


• **You want a credential employers recognize.** The completion credential travels with you from one employer to the next.


**The trade-offs of an apprenticeship:**


• **It's a long commitment.** Changing your mind in year two means walking away from a job, a wage schedule and a credential you've half earned.


• **Openings cluster in certain occupations.** Your target role may not have a registered program near you.


**An internship fits when:**


• **You're still comparing fields.** A short placement lets you test one before you commit, and most are built to fit a summer or a semester around a full course load.


• **Your target employers hire from their intern class.** Many large employers treat the internship as a long interview.


**The trade-offs of an internship:**


• **Pay isn't guaranteed.** Some placements are unpaid or pay only a small stipend, which can rule them out if you need the income.


• **Popular programs are hard to get.** If your resume is thin, start with our guide to[getting an internship with no experience](https://www.extern.com/post/how-to-get-internship-no-experience-guide) .


### What If Neither Fits Right Now?


Plenty of people land in between. They aren't ready to give years to one occupation, and they can't get, or can't fit, a full-time summer internship. What then?


Other formats cover that gap. A co-op is a longer, usually paid placement built into some degree programs. We compare it in[co-op vs internship](https://www.extern.com/post/co-op-vs-internship-guide) . An Externship is a short, remote professional experience built around a project and guided by an extern manager. Most run 8 weeks (the range is 4 to 11) at 5 to 10 hours a week, so they fit around classes. Our[externship vs internship](https://www.extern.com/post/externship-vs-internship-guide) comparison explains how the two differ.


At Extern, we've seen students use a short project to test a field before they commit to anything longer. In our post-program survey of 1,888 students (December 2025 to June 2026), 93.5% said they were satisfied or very satisfied with the experience. If e-commerce and data are on your list, the[Breaking Games E-Commerce Data Analysis & Strategy Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/breaking-games-e-commerce-data-analysis-strategy-oct-2026) is one example of what that looks like.


Your situation decides this far more than the label on the program does.


Your situation Best fit Why


**You have picked a skilled occupation and want to earn while you train** Registered apprenticeship Paid job, structured training and a national credential


**You are a full-time student comparing two or three fields** Internship Short, and built to fit a summer or semester


**You want a degree and a paycheck together** Degree apprenticeship Coursework tied to a paid role. Most common in teaching and nursing


**Your college builds full-time work terms into the degree** Co-op Longer placements that are usually paid


**You need something remote that fits around classes** Externship 4 to 11 weeks at 5 to 10 hours a week, project-based


**You have graduated and want to change careers** Registered apprenticeship, or an internship open to graduates Apprenticeships do not require college enrollment. Check each internship's eligibility

## How Do You List an Apprenticeship or Internship on a Resume?


Both go under Experience. The reason matters more than the rule, because it tells you where everything else on your resume belongs.


### The Background Check Test


**Where does an experience go on a resume?** Ask one question: can it be confirmed in an employment background check? If an organization will verify your dates and your role, the experience belongs under Experience. If all you have is a certificate of completion, it belongs under Projects or Certifications.


Apprenticeships and internships both pass that test, because the employer verifies them. Externships on Extern support employment background checks as well.


Here's how each entry looks:


• **Apprenticeship:** list it under Experience as a job, for example "IT Support Apprentice, Employer Name, March 2025 to present," with bullets on what you can now do without supervision. When you finish, add the completion credential under Certifications.


• **Internship:** list it under Experience with the employer, your title and the dates, for example "Marketing Intern, Employer Name, June to August 2026," with bullets on what you produced.


Our article on[resume claims and background checks](https://www.extern.com/post/lie-on-resume-background-check) explains what employers verify.


### How Recruiters Read Each One


We've spent years on the recruitment process outsourcing side, watching how employers screen early-career candidates. This is how the two lines tend to land.


An apprenticeship reads as a job. A recruiter sees tenure, a named employer and a credential showing that a third party checked your skills.


An internship reads as exposure, plus a signal that an employer picked you. Recruiters look at where it was, how long it lasted and, above all, what you produced. Internships are also a hiring pipeline. According to NACE's[2026 Internship & Co-op Report](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/internships/intern-conversion-rate-hits-highest-mark-in-five-years) , employers converted 63.1% of their 2024-25 interns into full-time hires.


Yet neither label rescues a vague entry. "Assisted with projects" tells a recruiter nothing, whichever heading sits above it.


If you're building a first resume, see our guide to writing a[resume with no experience](https://www.extern.com/post/resume-with-no-experience) . If you've completed an Externship, here's[how to list an Externship on your resume](https://www.extern.com/post/externship-on-resume-boosts-credibility) .


Many summer internship applications open in the fall. If you'd like a finished project to point to before then, you can[browse open Externships](https://www.extern.com/externships) .

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is an apprenticeship better than an internship?


Neither is better across the board. An apprenticeship is the stronger choice if you've picked an occupation and want a paid job with training and a credential. An internship fits better if you're still in school, still comparing fields, or need something that lasts one summer instead of one to three years.


### Do apprenticeships pay more than internships?


Over the full program, usually yes, because an apprenticeship is a job that lasts years and raises your wage as your skills grow. Hour for hour, it depends on the field. Interns at the bachelor's level averaged $23.35 an hour in NACE's 2026 compensation guide, and some internships are still unpaid. Registered apprentices are always paid.


### Can you do an apprenticeship while in college?


Sometimes. A degree apprenticeship combines a paid job with college coursework, so you earn a degree and an apprenticeship credential together. New America counted 579 of these options at 346 US colleges in 2025, most often for K-12 teaching and nursing. A standard full-time apprenticeship is hard to combine with a full course load.


### Does an apprenticeship count as work experience?


Yes. An apprenticeship is paid employment, so it goes in the Experience section of your resume with your employer, job title and dates, and the employer can confirm it in a background check. List the completion credential separately under Certifications. An internship also counts as experience and is verified the same way.


### How do I find a registered apprenticeship?


Start with the Apprenticeship Finder on Apprenticeship.gov, the US Department of Labor's site. Enter an occupation and a location to see open apprenticeship postings, then apply directly with the employer or program sponsor listed. Your state apprenticeship agency and local community colleges are also worth checking, since some programs partner with them.
